# Test-Driven Development

Prove that a test distinguishes the required behavior from the defect, then make the smallest coherent fix. Lightweight documentation does not waive regression evidence.

## When to use it

- For a reproducible behavior bug, establish a regression test before changing production behavior.
- Default to test-first for complex logic and permission, persistent-data, concurrency or compatibility boundaries. Follow stricter project rules.
- Plain documentation, instruction skills, generated assets or declarative configuration may need schema checks, realistic scenario evaluation or a safe execution check instead. Do not assert words/headings merely to manufacture a green test.
- Use this as the kit's TDD entrypoint. Honor an explicitly selected alternative without loading both. A user-requested exploration can remain throwaway without a complete test suite; keeping it as production behavior requires the appropriate checks.

## Red, green, refactor

1. Identify the observable contract, a boundary case that violates it, and the narrowest real test seam. Read existing callers and tests where they determine the contract.
2. Write/run the check on the unmodified behavior. Verify it fails for the intended assertion; an import error, unavailable service or missing fixture is not a demonstrated regression.
3. Change the root cause and rerun the same check. Include the valid-path behavior so rejecting all inputs cannot pass as a fix.
4. Add relevant failure/edge cases, then run affected integration and project-required checks. Refactor only within scope and rerun checks affected by that refactor.

Preserve existing implementation and user edits. If code was written first, prove the test's sensitivity against the original revision or a controlled broken variant in a separate temporary copy. Do not delete implementation, reset the checkout, or replay mutations in a shared environment to reconstruct red–green.

## Failure signals and next actions

| Signal | Required response |
| --- | --- |
| New regression test passes on the known-broken code | Check the assertion and the executed code path; no regression proof yet |
| Test mocks the changed decision itself | Exercise the decision through a real boundary; mocks may isolate external I/O |
| Fix makes the happy path pass but ignores rejected input or partial failure | Test the contract's relevant negative path and state after failure |
| Timing/retry change makes a flaky test pass | Establish an observable ordering/condition; do not hide the race with a larger sleep |
| Setup or shared-service access prevents safe red/green | Report the limitation and the best safe alternative; do not claim a reproduced fix |

Before finishing, identify the failing assertion/exit result, the post-fix result, and remaining scope limits in existing task evidence. Do not require a separate log document for a small task.

Read [writing-good-tests.md](writing-good-tests.md) when choosing assertions, mocks or test seams is uncertain. Keep useful tests stable across internal refactoring; do not insist that every helper have its own test.

# Optional Core Workflow Rules

This is a rule fragment for review and integration, not an automatically active global file. Adopt only clauses compatible with your project rules; resolve conflicts instead of appending a second workflow.

- Read project conventions and relevant code first. Reuse the existing spec, ADR, issue or task system and maintain one authoritative task-status source. Kiro is not required by default.
- Handle ordinary questions, read-only checks, wording edits and bounded low-risk fixes directly. Use design, planning, testing and review workflows where unresolved requirements, complexity or risk warrants them. Lightweight process does not waive relevant verification.
- Select skills by intent, not isolated keywords. Use one planning, debugging or TDD workflow rather than stacking equivalents; simple tasks may need no skill.
- Continue authorized implementation, relevant verification and in-scope repairs. Respect a request that ends at analysis, planning or preview. Existing authorization remains valid for the same object, action and scope.
- Do not infer permission to commit, push, deploy, destroy data, install production dependencies or change global settings from a generic completion request. Pause only work that depends on a genuinely missing decision and continue independent work.
- Follow execution choices permitted by the host, project and user. Without an explicit choice, work inline rather than asking a separate mode question. Delegation requires applicable authorization; relabeling the implementer is not independent review.
- For reproducible behavior defects, establish a regression check sensitive to the defect. Default to test-first for complex logic, permissions, data integrity, concurrency and compatibility. Never delete existing implementation to reconstruct the sequence; use an isolated comparison if needed.
- Validate instruction skills, declarative configuration and prose through suitable structural or scenario checks. Do not manufacture behavioral tests that merely assert wording exists.
- Review skipped/deleted tests, weakened assertions, lowered thresholds, broader exclusions, exceptions and unfinished implementation. Legitimate replacements need equivalent coverage or explicit risk evidence; keywords alone are not findings.
- Reuse verification only when code, configuration, dependencies and relevant environment still match. Changed inputs or newly uncovered risks justify affected checks. Reuse unchanged failure output rather than rerunning solely for formatting.
- Classify failures before acting. Fix task-caused failures, and authorized in-scope baseline failures that block explicitly required acceptance. Report out-of-scope blockers accurately rather than claiming all gates passed.
- Before claiming merge/release readiness for security, permissions, persistent data, concurrency or cross-module protocol changes, obtain independent review. Without delegation authorization, record pending human review and continue independent work. Record an explicitly accepted, project-permitted waiver as an exception, not a passed review.
- Modify only relevant content and protect user work and credentials. Use isolated data for local validation; shared QA, sandbox and cluster environments are not inherently free of side effects.
- Report actual outcomes, verification scope and remaining gaps. Test counts do not establish overall quality, and unmeasured speed improvements must not be claimed.
